items.scenario: Legal asks you to answer questions about termination rights in a 100-page vendor contract. The answers will go into a memo to the CFO.
items.question: Which prompting approach is most appropriate?
options: Ask 'summarise the termination risks' and paste Claude's result straight into the memo
Get verbatim clause quotes with pages first, answer only from them, check each quote
Ask Claude to answer from its general knowledge of standard termination clauses
Split the contract into ten parts and ask for a separate risk score for each part
items.explanation: Quote-first grounding makes the answer checkable, and the exact-string check catches near-quotes with altered figures. High-stakes document Q&A needs both.
distractors: An unsupported summary hides errors such as wrong numbers or missed clauses, with no way to check.
General knowledge isn't this contract; the memo needs this contract's terms.
Arbitrary chunk scores aren't grounded answers and lose cross-clause context.

items.scenario: Your Project instructions say 'all costs in EUR'. A teammate insists the Project instruction will always override anything typed in a message, so no testing is needed.
items.question: What is the Practitioner response?
options: Agree; Project instructions act as a hard lock on every later message in the Project
Agree, but only on Enterprise plans, where Project instructions are enforced
Design a deliberate conflict test (e.g. ask for USD) and record what actually happens
Move the rule into account-wide Instructions, which always win over the Project
items.explanation: Precedence between instruction layers is model behaviour, not a guaranteed lock. Test it with an observable conflict, run it more than once, and record the result.
distractors: Project instructions are weighted context, not an enforcement mechanism.
Plan tier doesn't turn instruction weighting into a lock.
Personal preferences sit below Project instructions, and moving the rule doesn't replace testing.

items.scenario: A week-long capacity analysis lives in one chat. By turn 70, Claude re-proposes an autoscaling option you rejected on Monday and ignores your 'no bullet points' rule.
items.question: What should you do?
options: Keep going in the same chat and restate both rules every few turns from now on
Write a handover (goal, decisions, constraints, next step) and start a fresh chat
Ask Claude to scroll back through the chat and re-read Monday's messages carefully
Switch to a model with a larger context window so that nothing gets forgotten
items.explanation: These are overflow symptoms: forgotten instructions and re-proposed rejected options. A curated handover gives the next chat a clean, correct state, with rejected options listed explicitly.
distractors: Restating adds more tokens to a polluted context and treats the symptom.
The material is already in context; the problem is dilution, not access.
Capacity isn't the issue; attention over a long, noisy history is.

items.scenario: To 'give Claude full context', an engineer adds 80 exported wiki pages (many from 2023) to an onboarding Project. New joiners now get answers describing the old architecture as current.
items.question: What is the root-cause fix?
options: Add 'prefer recent information' to the Project instructions and keep all 80 pages
Curate to current, owned documents with a refresh cadence, and have Claude cite files
Switch the Project to the most capable model so it can judge which of the pages are current
Tell new joiners to add 'as of 2026' to their questions so answers stay current
items.explanation: The context is the defect: stale material competes with current material, and retrieval can surface the wrong file. Curating to current, owned sources with citations fixes it at the source.
distractors: The stale pages still compete in retrieval, and the instruction can't tell which pages are stale.
A stronger model reading stale sources still answers from them.
Shifting the burden to every user doesn't remove the stale material.

items.scenario: You need Claude to compare one clause across three versions of a SOW. You plan to type the question first, then paste the three 30-page documents below it.
items.question: How should you structure the prompt?
options: Keep the question first so that Claude knows what to look for while it reads each file
Put the three documents first, tagged with version metadata, and the question last
Paste only the first version in full and describe the other two in a sentence each
Ask the question three times, once straight after each document, and compare
items.explanation: With long inputs, material first and question last gives better answers. The instructions are then the freshest tokens before generation and aren't buried under 90 pages.
distractors: A question buried above 90 pages of material is a known cause of weaker long-context answers.
Describing documents instead of providing them invites invented differences.
Repeating the question fragments the task and loses the cross-version comparison.

items.scenario: Client updates from the same Project read formal when Asha prompts and chatty when Ben does. Each blames the other's prompting style.
items.question: How should this be framed and fixed?
options: As a prompting skill gap: send Ben on a prompt-writing course before he writes more
As a context problem: put voice and audience in shared, versioned Project instructions
As a model problem: pin one model for the whole Project so both users get the same voice
As a memory problem: have both users reset memory so old preferences stop leaking
items.explanation: When two people's prompts contradict, the shared context isn't deciding the question. Fix it once in shared, reviewed instructions rather than policing individual prompts.
distractors: Training one person leaves the shared context undecided; the next person reintroduces the drift.
The same model follows whichever voice each prompt asks for.
Memory isn't what causes the voice split; the missing shared instruction is.

items.scenario: You tell Claude 'answer only from the attached runbook'. For a question the runbook doesn't cover, Claude still gives a confident, generic answer.
items.question: What change to the instruction most directly prevents this?
options: Add: 'If the runbook doesn't answer it, reply "not in the provided material"'
Repeat 'ONLY from the runbook' in capital letters at the start and end of the prompt
Raise the effort level for the chat so Claude reasons harder about the runbook
Shorten the runbook so Claude reads every remaining section more carefully
items.explanation: Closed-book instructions need an escape hatch. Without a sanctioned way to say 'not covered', the model fills gaps with plausible general knowledge.
distractors: Emphasis doesn't give the model a permitted alternative when the material is silent.
More reasoning doesn't change what the instruction permits when the source is silent.
Cutting the runbook removes context without addressing gap-filling.

items.scenario: An analyst on a confidential M&A engagement wants to do one exploratory analysis without it shaping any later chat. They normally keep memory on.
items.question: What is the most proportionate control?
options: Reset all memory before and after the session so that nothing from it carries forward
Use an incognito chat for that analysis, knowing it still appears in org exports
Turn off memory for the whole organisation before the analysis begins
Add 'forget this conversation' at the end of the chat so memory drops it
items.explanation: Match the scope of the control to the scope of the need: one chat calls for incognito. It isn't saved to history or memory, though it is still included in Team/Enterprise exports.
distractors: Resetting destroys useful memory to protect one chat; that's disproportionate.
An org-wide change for one person's single analysis is out of proportion and not theirs to make.
An instruction doesn't stop memory from being updated by the chat.

items.scenario: Claude returns five 'verbatim' quotes from a 60-page policy to support its answer. Exact-string search finds three; two are close paraphrases, and one of those changes '30 days' to '60 days'.
items.question: What does this tell you, and what should you do?
options: Quote-first grounding clearly doesn't work, so drop it and read the whole document yourself
Quoting makes errors checkable, not impossible: fix both, re-derive what relied on them
Two near-misses out of five is acceptable for internal work, so carry on as before
Ask Claude to confirm the quotes are verbatim this time, and accept its confirmation
items.explanation: Quotes are generated like any other output. The mechanical check is the control, and any conclusion that rested on a bad quote must be re-derived.
distractors: The technique did its job: it exposed the error cheaply. Dropping it loses that.
A changed number in a policy citation is a material error, not an acceptable miss.
Self-confirmation is not verification; only the source settles it.

items.scenario: A Project instruction says 'responses ≤200 words'. Your personal preference says 'be thorough, include all caveats'. Outputs flip unpredictably between terse and long across runs.
items.question: What is the most robust fix?
options: Delete your personal preference so that only the Project's length rule applies
Add a tie-break rule to the Project that names which rule wins and flags overruns
Raise the effort level so the model resolves the conflict more consistently each time
Run each prompt three times and keep whichever version you like the best
items.explanation: Unresolved conflicts between layers resolve unpredictably. Either remove the conflict or state explicitly which rule wins (for example, completeness beats length, with the overrun flagged), so the behaviour is predictable and visible.
distractors: This may remove useful defaults for other Projects and doesn't encode the intended priority here.
More reasoning doesn't decide a priority you haven't stated.
Cherry-picking runs hides the inconsistency instead of fixing it.
